lessons.title: What is HTML?
lessons.description: How browsers read HTML, tag syntax, and the structure every web page needs.
hints: Most elements need an opening tag and a matching closing tag with a forward slash, e.g. <title> and </title>.
Content you want to see on the page goes inside <body>. Information about the page, such as the <title>, goes inside <head>.
The <title> doesn't appear on the page itself. Check the title shown in the preview header instead.
Comments start with <!-- and end with -->. Anything between them is ignored by the browser.

lessons.title: Text Content
lessons.description: Headings, paragraphs, line breaks, whitespace and character entities.
hints: Headings go from <h1> (most important) to <h6> (least important). Don't skip levels, e.g. an <h2> should come before an <h3>.

Pressing Enter in your code doesn't create a new line on the page. Use separate

elements for new paragraphs, or
for a single line break.
Multiple spaces in your code collapse into one on the page. Only <pre> keeps your spacing exactly as typed.
To show a < or > character on the page, use the entities < and >. Entities always start with & and end with a semicolon.

lessons.title: Lists
lessons.description: Organising content with unordered and ordered lists.
hints: Use <ul> when the order doesn't matter (bullet points) and <ol> when it does (numbered steps).
Every item in a list must be wrapped in its own <li> element.
Only <li> elements can go directly inside a <ul> or <ol>. Put any other content inside an <li>.

lessons.title: Formatting and Nesting
lessons.description: Emphasising text with meaning, and placing elements correctly inside one another.
hints: Use <strong> for important text and <em> for stressed text. <b> and <i> only change appearance, without adding meaning.

Close elements in the reverse order you opened them:

text

, not

text

.
A nested list goes inside an <li> of the outer list, not directly inside the <ul> or <ol>.
Indenting nested elements makes it much easier to see what sits inside what. Press Tab to indent.

lessons.title: Attributes, Paths and Links
lessons.description: Adding extra information to elements, understanding file paths, and linking pages together.
hints: Attributes go inside the opening tag, written as name="value", e.g. <a href="https://www.example.com">.
Links to other websites need the full address, including https://.
To link to a section on the same page, give the target element an id and link to it with a # in front, e.g. href="#contact" links to id="contact".
Each id must be unique: only one element on the page can use it.

lessons.title: Images and Media
lessons.description: Adding images, captions, video and audio, and writing useful alternative text.
hints: has no closing tag. Everything it needs goes in its attributes, such as src and alt.
Good alt text describes what the image shows or does, as if you were describing it to someone who can't see it. Avoid starting with "Image of".
If your image doesn't appear, check the spelling and capitalisation of the file path in src.
Add the controls attribute to <video> and <audio> so users can play and pause them.

lessons.title: Tables
lessons.description: Presenting data in rows and columns with accessible table headers.
hints: Tables are built row by row: each <tr> is a row, and the cells go inside it.
Use <th> for header cells and <td> for data cells.
Header rows go inside <thead> and data rows go inside <tbody>.
If your columns don't line up, check that every row has the same number of cells.

lessons.title: Grouping Content
lessons.description: Using div and span, understanding block and inline elements, and naming elements with class.
hints: Use <div> to group block-level content, such as several paragraphs. Use <span> to mark part of a line of text.
Block elements start on a new line and take up the full width. Inline elements sit within a line of text.
Unlike id, a class can be used on many elements, and one element can have several classes separated by spaces, e.g. class="card featured".
<div> and <span> don't change how your page looks on their own. Their purpose is to group content for styling later.

lessons.title: Semantic Structure
lessons.description: Structuring pages with meaningful elements, and why semantics matter for accessibility.
hints: A page should have only one <main> element, containing its primary content.
Use <nav> for groups of navigation links, not for every link on the page.
Use <article> for content that would make sense on its own, such as a blog post. Use <section> for a themed part of a larger page.
Ask yourself what each part of the page is, not what it looks like. If no semantic element fits, a <div> is fine.

lessons.title: Forms and Buttons
lessons.description: Collecting user input with labelled form fields and buttons.
hints: Connect each <label> to its input by matching the label's for attribute to the input's id.
Give every input a name attribute. This is how the data is identified when the form is submitted.
Choose the input type that matches the data, e.g. type="email" or type="number". The browser will help check it for you.
A <button> inside a form submits it by default. Use type="button" for a button that shouldn't submit.

lessons.title: Consolidation: Build and Validate
lessons.description: Bring everything together in a complete semantic page and check it with the W3C validator.
hints: Plan your page structure first: what goes in the <header>, <main> and <footer>?
Validate by copying all of your HTML and pasting it into the "Validate by Direct Input" tab of the W3C validator.
Fix validator errors from the top down. One early mistake, such as an unclosed tag, can cause several errors further down.
Warnings are suggestions rather than errors, but they are still worth reading.
